questions.question: Six months into a CRM project, sales leadership reorganizes territories twice, and each reorganization forces edits to 40 agreed requirements. What is the name given to this chronic instability in stakeholder needs?
questions.explanation: Volatility is the tendency of requirements to change as stakeholders' understanding and business conditions evolve - tracked via a change/volatility rate.

questions.question: For a railway interlocking subsystem, ambiguous prose is unacceptable; the team specifies behavior with Z schemas and set-theoretic pre/postconditions that a tool can check. Which requirements technique is this?
questions.explanation: Formal specification expresses requirements in a mathematically grounded notation (Z, VDM, B) so properties can be verified, not just reviewed.

questions.question: An order can move Pending -> Paid -> Shipped -> Delivered, or be Cancelled from Pending only. Which modeling artifact captures the allowed states and the events that transition between them?
questions.explanation: A state (machine) diagram models an object's lifecycle as states plus event-triggered transitions - exactly the Pending/Paid/Shipped lifecycle here.

questions.question: Analysts walk through 'customer abandons cart mid-payment' and 'network drops during checkout' storylines to extract requirements that stakeholder interviews missed. Which analysis technique is this?
questions.explanation: Scenario analysis works through concrete usage situations - including failure and edge stories - to surface requirements interviews overlook.

questions.question: After change-control board sign-off, SRS v2.0 is frozen and every future change request must be evaluated against that approved snapshot. What is the frozen SRS v2.0 called?
questions.explanation: A baseline is the agreed, controlled version of the requirements; changes after it must pass formal change control.

questions.question: A requirement demands 10 ms end-to-end image processing on hardware that benchmarks prove needs 40 ms. Which requirements quality attribute does it violate?
questions.explanation: A requirement must be implementable within technical, schedule, and budget constraints; one the hardware cannot physically meet is infeasible.

questions.question: An analysis team models the payroll system with data flow diagrams, a data dictionary, and process mini-specs rather than object models. Which classic requirements modeling approach is this?
questions.explanation: Structured analysis (DeMarco/Yourdon) decomposes a system into processes, data flows, data stores, and dictionaries - the pre-UML modeling school.

questions.question: Marketing insists on feature X, support demands feature Y, and the budget covers only one; the team scores both against value, risk, and cost to settle it. Which requirements activity resolves this conflict?
questions.explanation: Prioritization ranks competing requirements on value, cost, and risk (MoSCoW, AHP, voting) so disagreements resolve into an ordered backlog.

questions.question: A review board rejects 'the system shall respond quickly' because no tester could objectively pass or fail it. Which quality criterion is the requirement missing?
questions.explanation: A verifiable requirement supplies a measurable criterion - e.g., 'p95 < 200 ms' - so conformance can be checked by test or inspection.

questions.question: A change request alters requirement R-42, and the PM must list every design element, code module, and test case that could be affected. Which artifact records those links?
questions.explanation: A traceability matrix maps each requirement forward to design, code, and tests and back to stakeholder needs, enabling impact analysis.

questions.question: The correct sequence of the four core requirements engineering activities, from first to last.
questions.explanation: Requirements are elicited from stakeholders, analyzed for conflicts, specified in documents like the SRS, then validated for correctness.

questions.question: A hospital system must maintain 99.999% uptime. In the FURPS classification, which letter covers this kind of requirement?
questions.explanation: In FURPS (Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability), uptime and availability fall under Reliability.

questions.question: Reviewing a spec, an analyst files 'must run on the existing Oracle 19c database' and 'must integrate with corporate SSO' under neither Reliability nor Performance. In FURPS+, under which category do these belong?
questions.explanation: FURPS+ adds a '+' for constraints: design, implementation, interface, and physical restrictions that limit the solution space.

questions.question: A legacy payroll system has undocumented rules that exist only in its code. Which technique recovers requirements by analyzing that code?
questions.explanation: Reverse engineering examines existing code and behavior to reconstruct requirements when documentation is absent or outdated.

questions.question: The top-level requirement 'detect intrusions within 2 seconds' must be split so the sensor-hardware team and the analytics-software team each know the share they own. What is this process of flowing system requirements down to subsystems called?
questions.explanation: Allocation apportions each system requirement to specific subsystems or components, so every architectural element owns defined responsibilities.

questions.question: In a use case, the scenario 'user enters a wrong PIN three times and the card is retained' is documented separately from the successful basic flow as this kind of flow.
questions.explanation: Deviations from the happy path are captured as alternative/exception flows; the locking scenario is an alternative flow of the ATM use case.

questions.question: DSDM/MoSCoW guidance says Must-haves should total no more than about 60% of effort. A 60-point backlog assigns 40 points to Musts. State whether it complies, and the maximum allowed.
questions.answer: No - Musts must be at most ~36 points (60% of 60); 40 exceeds it
questions.explanation: 60% of 60 points = 36 points; assigning 40 points to Must-haves breaks the guideline meant to keep contingency for lower-priority features.

questions.question: 'The system shall be user-friendly.' Name the two quality criteria this requirement most clearly violates.
questions.explanation: 'User-friendly' has multiple possible interpretations (not unambiguous) and gives no measurable criterion to test against (not verifiable).

questions.question: In a library domain model, a Loan links Member and Book but itself carries attributes such as due date and renewal count. The UML construct that attaches attributes to a relationship.
questions.explanation: An association class lets an association itself own attributes and operations - exactly what is needed when the relationship (Loan) has state.

questions.question: An NFR reads 'p95 response time < 200 ms at 5,000 concurrent users.' The name for the measurable threshold used to objectively test whether a non-functional requirement has been met.
questions.explanation: The fit criterion quantifies an NFR (e.g., 'p95 < 200 ms @ 5,000 users') so testers can objectively decide pass/fail.
